headline: Return one branch; score both branches
statement: Find the largest sum of values on any nonempty simple path in a binary tree. Consecutive path nodes must share a parent-child edge. The path may start and end anywhere and need not contain the root.
intuition: A path may pass through a node and use both of its child branches. But a path extended to the node's parent can use only one child branch. Calculate both quantities separately: the best complete path through this node, and the best single branch to pass upward.
approach: Use an explicit postorder stack to visit children before their parent.
Read each child’s best downward gain and clip negative gains to zero.
Score a path through the node using both gains, then store one-branch gain for its parent.
correctness: Every simple tree path has a unique highest node. At that node, its two downward parts are optimized by the child gains, and including a negative part cannot help. Evaluating every possible highest node finds the best path; storing only one branch ensures a parent extension remains a path.
bruteForce: Try every pair of endpoints and compute their connecting path, costing up to O(n³) without additional preprocessing.

complexity.explanation: Explicit postorder avoids Python recursion limits; gains and traversal storage are linear.

pitfalls: A parent can extend only one child branch.
Initialize best below every possible node value so all-negative trees work.
The answer must contain at least one node.
